## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100258.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100258.3.sa2)

This study by Tardiff, Kang & Gold seeks to (i) develop a normative account of how observers should adapt their decision-making across environments with different levels of correlation between successive pairs of observations, and (ii) assess whether human decisions in such environments are consistent with this normative model. The authors first demonstrate that, in the range of environments under consideration here, an observer with full knowledge of the generative statistics should take both the magnitude and sign of the underlying correlation into account when assigning weight in their decisions to new observations: stronger negative correlations should translate into stronger weighting (due to the greater information furnished by an anticorrelated generative source), while stronger positive correlations should translate into weaker weighting (due to the greater redundancy of information provided by a positively correlated generative source). The authors then report an empirical study in which human participants performed a perceptual decision-making task requiring accumulation of information provided by pairs of perceptual samples, under different levels of pairwise correlation. They describe a nuanced pattern of results with effects of correlation being largely restricted to response times and not choice accuracy, which could be captured through fits of their normative model (in this implementation, an extension of the well-known drift diffusion model) to the participants' behaviour while allowing for mis-estimation of the underlying correlations. An intriguing result is that the observed pattern of behavioural effects is best explained by a model in which observers marginally underestimated the level of correlation between the generative sources, and that this bias affects behaviour through effects on stimulus encoding that then shape how the evidence furnished by each stimulus sample is weighted in decision formation.

As the authors point out in their very well-written paper, appropriate weighting of information gathered in correlated environments has important consequences for real-world decision-making. Yet, while this function has been well studied for 'high-level' (e.g. economic) decisions, how we account for correlations when making simple perceptual decisions on well-controlled behavioural tasks has not been investigated. As such, this study addresses an important and timely question that will be of broad interest to psychologists and neuroscientists. The computational approach to arrive at normative principles for evidence weighting across environments with different levels of correlation is elegant, makes strong connections with prior work in different decision-making contexts, and should serve as a valuable reference point for future studies in this domain. The empirical study is well designed and executed, and the modelling approach applied to these data showcases an impressively deep understanding of relationships between different parameters of the drift diffusion model and its novel application to this setting. Another strength of the study is that it is preregistered.

In my view, any major weaknesses of the study have been well addressed by the authors during review. An outstanding question that arises from the current work and remains unanswered here is around the (normative?) origin of the correlation underestimates, and the present work lays a strong foundation from which to pursue this question in the future.

claims.source: The models that did not include correlation-dependent bound adjustments (the base and drift models) provided poor fits to the data (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 3), underscoring the importance of changes in evidence weighing rather than simply changes in subjective stimulus strength for capturing the participants' performance.
claims.evidence: Model comparison results shown in Figure 6a and supplement.

claims.claim: There was a strong relationship between the objective and subjective correlations used by each participant.
claims.source: There was a strong relationship between the objective and subjective correlations used by each participant (Figure 7a; B=0.71, t(99)=47.92, p<0.001, Fisher z-transformed scale).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of fit parameters shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: Participants were sensitive to the correlations and used them to adjust their decision process.
claims.source: This result confirms that the participants were sensitive to the correlations and used them to adjust their decision process.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the strong relationship between objective and subjective correlations.

claims.claim: The fit (subjective) correlations tended to be more variable for positive versus negative correlations.
claims.source: The fit (subjective) correlations also tended to be more variable for positive versus negative correlations (Figure 7a; mean value of the standard deviation of Fisher z-transformed estimates = 0.20 for positive correlation conditions, 0.09 for negative correlation conditions), possibly reflecting the weaker consequences of misestimating positive versus negative correlations on performance (Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: Analysis of variability in fit parameters shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: Overall performance was much closer to ideal than if the participants ignored the correlations when computing the weight of evidence.
claims.source: Despite these suboptimalities, overall performance was much closer to ideal (i.e., perfect encoding and use of the correlation) than if the participants ignored the correlations when computing the weight of evidence (Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: Comparison of performance to ideal and naïve observers shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: Empirical correlations tended to be biased toward zero when based on a very limited number of samples.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, these empirical correlations tended to be biased toward zero when based on a very limited number of samples, as expected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Zimmerman et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation.

claims.claim: There was no reliable evidence that participants with the shortest average RTs tended to have subjective estimates that were most strongly biased towards zero.
claims.source: Contrary to this prediction, we found no reliable evidence that participants with the shortest average RTs (and thus who observed the fewest samples) tended to have subjective estimates that were most strongly biased towards zero (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The participants did not compute the correlation explicitly on each trial.
claims.source: These results suggest that the participants did not compute the correlation explicitly on each trial and thus instead might have used pattern matching (e.g., quickly assessing if the first few samples seem consistent with other observations from the negative-, zero-, or positive-correlation stimuli they already observed) or other heuristics to make correlation-dependent adjustments to the decision process.
claims.evidence: Inference from the lack of relationship between empirical and subjective correlations.

claims.claim: The participants tended to exhibit some learning over the course of the task, involving substantial decreases in RT.
claims.source: In particular, the participants tended to exhibit some learning over the course of the task, involving substantial decreases in RT (the mean ± SEM difference in RT between the first and second half of the task, measured across participants, was 0.71±0.06 s, respectively, Mann–Whitney test for H0: median difference = 0, p<0.001) at the expense of only slight decreases in accuracy (0.02 ± 0.00% correct, p=0.004).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of learning effects.

claims.claim: Learning trends reflected a tendency to use slightly higher drift rates and lower decision bounds in the latter half of the task.
claims.source: These trends reflected a tendency to use slightly higher drift rates (Figure 8a) and lower decision bounds (Figure 8b) in the latter half of the task, a pattern of results that is consistent with previous reports of practice effects for simple decisions (Balci et al., 2011; Dutilh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 8 and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Learning adjustments were not accompanied by similar, systematic adjustments in the participants' subjective correlation estimates.
claims.source: However, these adjustments were not accompanied by similar, systematic adjustments in the participants' subjective correlation estimates, which were similar in the first versus second half of the task (Figure 8c).
claims.evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 8c.

claims.claim: Participants' decisions appeared to be based on relatively stable estimates of the stimulus correlations that could be determined and used effectively on a trial-by-trial basis.
claims.source: Thus, participants' decisions appeared to be based on relatively stable estimates of the stimulus correlations that could be determined and used effectively on a trial-by-trial basis.
claims.evidence: Inference from the stability of correlation estimates across task halves.

claims.claim: Human participants make decisions that are approximately consistent with using the normative logLR that accounts for correlations.
claims.source: We showed that human participants make decisions that are approximately consistent with using this normative quantity, mitigating changes in decision speed and/or accuracy that would result from ignoring correlations.
claims.evidence: Summary of main findings.

claims.claim: Perceptual reports based on cues from multiple sensory modalities often reflect weights of evidence that scale with the relative reliability of each cue, consistent with Bayesian theory.
claims.source: Perceptual reports based on cues from multiple sensory modalities, or multiple cues from the same modality, often reflect weights of evidence that scale with the relative reliability of each cue, consistent with Bayesian theory (Ernst, 2005; Noppeney, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: The relationship between speed and accuracy for many decisions can be captured by models like the DDM that assume accumulating quantities that are often assumed to be (scaled) versions of the logLR.
claims.source: The relationship between speed and accuracy for many decisions can be captured by models like the DDM that assume that the underlying decision process involves accumulating quantities that are often assumed to be (scaled) versions of the logLR (Bogacz et al., 2006; Edwards, 1965; Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Laming, 1968; Stone, 1960).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Using an appropriate, multiplicative scale factor to compute the weight of evidence can support normative decision-making as long as there is a linear relationship between subjective stimulus strength and logLR.
claims.source: Thus, as long as there is a linear relationship between subjective stimulus strength and logLR, then using an appropriate, multiplicative scale factor to compute the weight of evidence (either scaling the observations or the bound, depending on the particular algorithmic implementation) can support normative decision-making.
claims.evidence: Theoretical statement about decision-making models.

claims.claim: Results from studies using paradigms where objective stimulus strength is held constant within blocks have been mixed, including bounds that do or do not vary across blocks.
claims.source: Results from studies using these paradigms have been mixed, including bounds that do (Malhotra et al., 2017; Starns and Ratcliff, 2012) or do not (Balci et al., 2011) vary across blocks.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Several studies found that people deviate from optimal to a greater degree in low-stimulus-strength conditions because they value accuracy and not solely reward rate.
claims.source: For example, several studies found that people deviate from optimal to a greater degree in low-stimulus-strength conditions because they value accuracy and not solely reward rate (Balci et al., 2011; Bohil and Maddox, 2003; Starns and Ratcliff, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Deviations from optimal bounds can depend on the uncertainty with which task timing is estimated, rather than uncertainty in estimates of stimulus strength.
claims.source: Additionally, deviations from optimal bounds can depend on the uncertainty with which task timing is estimated, rather than uncertainty in estimates of stimulus strength (Zacksenhouse et al., 2010), suggesting that people can estimate stimulus strength even if they do not use it as prescribed by reward-rate maximization.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to relevant literature.

claims.claim: The standard SPRT and the DDM are no longer optimal when objective stimulus strength is varied from trial-to-trial.
claims.source: Under these conditions, the standard SPRT, and the DDM as its continuous-time equivalent (Bogacz et al., 2006), are no longer optimal (Deneve, 2012; Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Moran, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: It is possible to adjust how decisions are formed about stimuli whose statistics vary from trial to trial, in a manner that is consistent with trying to use optimal (or near-optimal) forms of the weight of evidence.
claims.source: However, several modeling and empirical studies have shown that it is possible to adjust how decisions are formed about stimuli whose statistics vary from trial to trial, in a manner that is consistent with trying to use optimal (or near-optimal) forms of the weight of evidence.
claims.evidence: Supported by subsequent citations.

claims.claim: Under certain conditions, human decision-making behavior is consistent with making adjustments using decision bounds that 'collapse' over time.
claims.source: Under certain conditions, human decision-making behavior is consistent with making such adjustments, for example by using decision bounds that 'collapse' over time (Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Malhotra et al., 2017; Palestro et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Outside relatively simple cases involving statistically independent observations, elapsed time cannot serve as a sole proxy for stimulus strength.
claims.source: Our results imply that outside relatively simple cases involving statistically independent observations, elapsed time cannot serve as a sole proxy for stimulus strength.
claims.evidence: Inference from the study results.

claims.claim: Correlations between pairs of observations can complicate the relationship between the strength of evidence provided by individual observations and elapsed time.
claims.source: In particular, correlations between pairs of observations can complicate the relationship between the strength of evidence provided by individual observations and elapsed time.
claims.evidence: Inference from the study results.

claims.claim: In more general settings elapsed time should be combined with other relevant statistics, such as the correlation, to determine an appropriate weight of evidence.
claims.source: Therefore, in more general settings elapsed time should be combined with other relevant statistics, such as the correlation, to determine an appropriate weight of evidence.
claims.evidence: Inference from the study results.

claims.claim: The data are consistent with decisions that used collapsing bounds, which helped adjust the decision process when the objective evidence strength changed within each correlation condition.
claims.source: In support of this idea, our data are consistent with decisions that used collapsing bounds, which helped adjust the decision process when the objective evidence strength changed within each correlation condition (i.e., the low and high values of evidence strength that corresponded to substantial modulations of the psychometric and chronometric functions).
claims.evidence: Inference from model fitting results.

claims.claim: Collapsing bounds alone, without additional correlation-dependent computations, could not account for the behavioral results.
claims.source: However, collapsing bounds alone, without additional correlation-dependent computations, could not account for our behavioral results, which by design used values of objective evidence strength that did not change across correlation conditions.
claims.evidence: Inference from model comparison results.

claims.claim: The results are in stark contrast with the literature on correlations in behavioral economics, which suggests that people fail to use correlations appropriately to inform their decision-making.
claims.source: Our results are in stark contrast with the literature on correlations in behavioral economics, which suggests that people fail to use correlations appropriately to inform their decision-making.
claims.evidence: Comparison to prior literature.

claims.claim: When combining information from multiple sources, most participants exhibit 'correlation neglect', which often leads to reduced decision accuracy.
claims.source: For example, when combining information from multiple sources (e.g., for financial forecasts: Budescu and Yu, 2007; Enke and Zimmermann, 2017; Hossain and Okui, 2021; Maines, 1996; Maines, 1990; or constructing portfolios of correlated assets: Eyster and Weizsacker, 2016; Laudenbach et al., 2023), most participants exhibit 'correlation neglect' (i.e., partially or fully failing to account for correlations), which often leads to reduced decision accuracy.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Positive correlations have been proposed to lead to overconfidence, which has been attributed to failing to account for redundancy.
claims.source: Positive correlations have also been proposed to lead to overconfidence, which has been attributed to failing to account for redundancy (Eyster and Rabin, 2010; Glaeser and Sunstein, 2009; Ortoleva and Snowberg, 2015) or to the false assumption that consistency among information sources suggests higher reliability (Kahneman and Tversky, 1973).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: Discrepant results between this study and behavioral economics studies are likely a result of the vast differences in task designs.
claims.source: These discrepant results are likely a result of the vast differences in task designs between those studies and ours.
claims.evidence: Inference about reasons for different findings.

claims.claim: Highly simplified task structures increase the ability to account for correlations.
claims.source: Nevertheless, even in simplified cases, decisions in descriptive scenarios likely rely on very different cognitive mechanisms than decisions that, like ours, are based directly on relatively simple sensory stimuli.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation.

claims.claim: Decisions under risk can vary substantially when based on description versus direct experience.
claims.source: For example, decisions under risk can vary substantially when based on description versus direct experience (Hertwig and Erev, 2009), and giving passive exposure to samples from distributions underlying two correlated assets can alleviate correlation neglect in subsequent allocation decisions (Laudenbach et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: When combining multiple visual cues to estimate slant, some observers' estimates are consistent with assuming a correlation between cues.
claims.source: For example, when combining multiple visual cues to estimate slant, some observers' estimates are consistent with assuming a correlation between cues, which is sensible because the cues derive from the same retinal image and likely overlapping populations of neurons (Oruç et al., 2003; Rosas et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: The combination of within-modality cues is thought to be encapsulated within the visual system, such that observers have no conscious access to the individual cues.
claims.source: The combination of within-modality cues is thought to be encapsulated within the visual system, such that observers have no conscious access to the individual cues (Girshick and Banks, 2009; Hillis et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: The visual system may have specialized mechanisms for computing correlations among visual stimuli that are different than those used to support higher-order cognition.
claims.source: These results suggest that the visual system may have specialized mechanisms for computing correlations among visual stimuli (which may or may not involve the well-studied, but different, phenomena of correlations in the patterns of firing rates of individual neurons; Cohen and Kohn, 2011) that are different than those used to support higher-order cognition.
claims.evidence: Inference from prior literature with citation.

claims.claim: Suboptimal evidence weighing reflected subjective misestimates of the correlation at the level of encoding.
claims.source: Given our finding that suboptimal evidence weighing reflected subjective misestimates of the correlation at the level of encoding, these putative encoding mechanisms appear to be tightly coupled to those that convert observations into a weight of evidence.
claims.evidence: Inference from model fitting results.

claims.claim: Human decision-makers' sensitivity to correlations does not seem to require extensive, task-specific learning and can be adjusted flexibly from one decision to the next.
claims.source: We showed that this impact can be substantial for a particular form of correlation, and that human decision-makers' sensitivity to correlations does not seem to require extensive, task-specific learning and can be adjusted flexibly from one decision to the next.
claims.evidence: Summary of main findings.

results.result: The normative weight of evidence for paired observations from correlated Gaussian random variables depends systematically on the sign and magnitude of the correlation. Negative correlations provide stronger evidence with increasing magnitude, while positive correlations provide weaker evidence with increasing magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 present a theoretical derivation shown in Figure 1 that establishes the mathematical relationship between correlation and evidence weight. The theoretical analysis is mathematically sound and provides the foundation for the experimental design.

results.result: The experimental design adjusted generative distribution means to equate expected logLR (objective evidence strength) across correlation conditions. This design allows differentiation between participants who use true logLR (producing identical choices and RTs across correlations) versus those who ignore correlations (showing systematic biases).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 describe the experimental design manipulation that is central to testing the study's hypotheses. The design is theoretically sound and appropriately controls for confounds, as shown in Figure 2.

results.result: Participants' choice accuracy was affected by evidence strength but not correlation, while response times were affected by both evidence strength and correlation. Choices did not vary across correlation conditions, consistent with accounting for correlations, but RTs showed correlation-dependent patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 present behavioral results supported by statistical analyses (logistic models, mixed-effects models) with appropriate significance tests. The pattern of results is consistent across individual and aggregate data (Figures 3a, 3b), providing strong empirical support.

results.result: The RT data imply that participants' use of correlations was not optimal (not equivalent to true logLR) because RTs varied by correlation condition. The RT patterns were consistent with decisions based on approximations of logLR using underestimates of the correlation-dependent scale factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 provide inference from the RT data patterns and comparison to theoretical predictions. The qualitative match between data and simulations (Figure 4) supports the interpretation, though quantitative model fitting provides stronger evidence in subsequent results.

results.result: Participants' behavior was consistent with an accumulate-to-bound process scaled on each trial based on normative, correlation-dependent evidence weighing using slight misestimates of correlation. Models without correlation-dependent bound adjustments provided poor fits.
results.evaluation: Claims C46 and C48 are supported by formal model comparison showing the full-ρ^ model best captured behavior (Figure 6a). The model comparison uses appropriate statistical methods (AIC, protected exceedance probability) and the results are clear and consistent.

results.result: There was a strong relationship between objective and subjective correlations (B=0.71, p<0.001), confirming that participants were sensitive to correlations and used them to adjust their decision process.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 present statistical analysis of model fit parameters with appropriate significance testing. The strong correlation and highly significant p-value provide clear evidence for the relationship (Figure 7a).

results.result: Subjective correlations were more variable for positive versus negative correlations, possibly reflecting weaker consequences of misestimating positive correlations. Despite suboptimalities, performance was much closer to ideal than if correlations were ignored.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 present analysis of parameter variability and performance comparison to ideal and naïve observers. The results are supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7, though the explanation for differential variability is speculative.

results.result: Empirical correlations computed from observed samples were biased toward zero with limited samples, but participants did not appear to compute correlations explicitly on each trial. Instead, they may have used pattern matching or other heuristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 present analyses testing whether participants computed empirical correlations trial-by-trial. The lack of relationship between RT and subjective estimates (C55) and between empirical and subjective correlations (C57) supports the conclusion, though the alternative mechanisms proposed are speculative.

results.result: Participants exhibited learning over the task (decreased RT with minimal accuracy cost), reflected in higher drift rates and lower bounds in the second half. However, subjective correlation estimates remained stable across task halves, suggesting decisions were based on stable correlation estimates used trial-by-trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 present analysis of learning effects with appropriate statistical tests. The dissociation between changes in drift/bound parameters and stability of correlation estimates (Figure 8) supports the interpretation that correlation sensitivity does not require extensive learning.

results.result: Human participants make decisions approximately consistent with using normative logLR that accounts for correlations, and this sensitivity to correlations does not require extensive task-specific learning and can be adjusted flexibly trial-by-trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C87 summarize the main findings, which are well-supported by the convergent evidence from behavioral data, model fitting, and learning analyses presented throughout the results section.

results.result: Outside simple cases with independent observations, elapsed time cannot serve as sole proxy for stimulus strength because correlations complicate this relationship. Elapsed time should be combined with other statistics like correlation to determine appropriate evidence weight.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 present implications of the study results for understanding evidence accumulation. The inference is well-supported by the experimental findings showing that correlation-dependent adjustments beyond time-based calibration are necessary.

results.result: The data are consistent with decisions using collapsing bounds to adjust for evidence strength changes within correlation conditions, but collapsing bounds alone could not account for behavioral results across correlation conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 present inference from model fitting results. The conclusion is supported by the experimental design (constant objective evidence across correlations) and model comparison showing that correlation-dependent computations are necessary beyond collapsing bounds.

results.result: The results contrast with behavioral economics literature showing correlation neglect, likely due to vast differences in task designs. Simplified perceptual tasks may engage different mechanisms than descriptive decision scenarios.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 discuss the relationship between current findings and prior literature. The comparison is appropriately supported by citations, and the proposed explanation for discrepant results (task design differences) is reasonable, though the specific mechanisms remain speculative.

results.result: The visual system may have specialized mechanisms for computing correlations among visual stimuli that differ from those supporting higher-order cognition. Suboptimal evidence weighing reflected subjective misestimates at the encoding level, suggesting tight coupling between encoding and evidence conversion mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 present speculation about neural mechanisms based on comparison to prior literature and the current findings. While the inference about encoding-level misestimates (C86) is supported by model fitting, the claims about specialized visual mechanisms (C85) are speculative and would require neural data to support.

results.result: Background on normative decision-making principles: The brain forms deliberative decisions following normative principles related to evidence weighing and accumulation. The logLR is central to optimal decision models like SPRT and DDM, though it can be difficult to compute and may be approximated using heuristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge in the field and set up the study's motivation.

results.result: Non-independence of observations can substantially affect evidence weighing for effective decisions, with real-world consequences. Whether and how people account for correlations in perceptual decisions is not well understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C22 establish the knowledge gap and motivation for the study, supported by citations to relevant literature and theoretical analysis (Figure 1). The claims accurately represent the state of knowledge and justify the research question.

results.result: Discussion of prior work on evidence weighing: Previous research shows humans can weigh evidence normatively in cue combination and evidence accumulation tasks. However, results on whether people adjust bounds for stimulus strength have been mixed, and standard models are not optimal when stimulus strength varies trial-to-trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C71 provide discussion context supported by appropriate citations. The claims accurately represent prior literature and its relationship to the current findings, though some nuances about mixed results (C66) could benefit from more detailed discussion.

results.result: One hundred human participants took part in the online study with specified demographics.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 provides basic methodological information about the study sample. The sample size is adequate for the analyses performed, though no power analysis is reported to justify this specific number.

results.result: Main findings summary: Correlations in observations can dramatically impact evidence weight. With minimal training, participants adapted to trial-by-trial correlation changes and produced decisions based on approximately normative evidence weighing and accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 summarize the main findings, which are well-supported by the detailed results presented in the manuscript. These abstract-level claims accurately represent the empirical findings.

results.result: The study establishes the normative theoretical framework showing that correlations in observations have a dramatic impact on the weight of evidence. Specifically, negative correlations provide stronger evidence with increasing magnitude, while positive correlations provide weaker evidence with increasing magnitude, as illustrated in Figure 1.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this theoretical contribution. The editor states the work 'demonstrate[s] convincingly how humans make decisions about sequences of pairs of correlated observations.' Reviewer 1 praises 'the computational approach to arrive at normative principles for evidence weighting across environments with different levels of correlation is elegant.' Reviewer 2 similarly notes 'the authors first demonstrate that...an observer with full knowledge of the generative statistics should take both the magnitude and sign of the underlying correlation into account.'

results.result: The experimental design adjusted the means of generative distributions to ensure constant expected logLR (objective evidence strength) across correlation conditions. This design allowed prediction that normative decision-makers would show identical choices and RTs across correlations, while those ignoring correlations would show systematic biases.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises this design: 'the design allowed the authors to make the amount of decision-related evidence equal across different correlation magnitudes, which makes it easy to assess whether participants correctly take account of these correlations.' Reviewer 2 notes the study is 'well designed and executed.' No reviewer raises concerns about the experimental design logic.

results.result: Participants' choice accuracy was affected by objective evidence strength but not by correlation. Logistic model comparisons showed no benefit to fitting separate models per correlation condition, indicating choices did not vary across correlation conditions as expected for decisions accounting for correlations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'While Tardiff and colleagues found no impact of correlations on choices, they did find them to impact reaction times' and later confirms 'a consistent mis-estimation of the correlation magnitude would not impact the fraction of correct choices (as they observe).' Reviewer 2 describes this as part of 'a nuanced pattern of results with effects of correlation being largely restricted to response times and not choice accuracy.' No reviewer questions these choice findings.

results.result: Response times were affected by both evidence strength and correlation, with faster responses for stronger evidence and more positive correlations. Statistical analyses confirmed significant effects of correlation sign and its interaction with magnitude. These RT patterns imply the influence of correlations on decisions was not fully optimal.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges 'they did find them to impact reaction times, suggesting that participants deviated from the normative decision strategy.' Reviewer 2 describes 'effects of correlation being largely restricted to response times and not choice accuracy' as part of the key findings. The editor affirms the work 'demonstrate[s] convincingly' the decision-making patterns. No reviewer disputes the RT findings or their interpretation.

results.result: With minimal training, participants adapted to uncued trial-by-trial changes in correlations and produced decisions based on approximately normative weighing and accumulation of evidence. Behavior was consistent with an accumulate-to-bound process scaled on each trial according to a slight misestimate of the correlation, demonstrating sensitivity to correlations that could be adjusted flexibly.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Tardiff et al. conclude that participants followed a close-to normative decision strategy that adequately took into account correlated evidence' and praises that 'Limited training makes it more likely that the observed behavior is natural.' Reviewer 2 describes 'An intriguing result is that the observed pattern of behavioural effects is best explained by a model in which observers marginally underestimated the level of correlation.' The editor calls this 'important work' that demonstrates the findings 'convincingly.'

results.result: Participants' RTs were relatively constant or slightly decreasing with increasing correlations, particularly for larger correlations. These trends were inconsistent with ignoring correlations or using the true logLR with fixed bounds, but could be matched qualitatively to simulations using underestimates of the correlation-dependent scale factor.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly discusses how 'the authors showed that a consistent mis-estimation of the correlation magnitude would not impact the fraction of correct choices (as they observe), but only the reaction times' and confirms 'they could show that participants in fact performed rational evidence weighting if one assumed that they slightly underestimated the correlation magnitude.' No reviewer challenges these simulation-based inferences.

results.result: Model comparison showed that models without correlation-dependent bound adjustments provided poor fits. The best-fitting model revealed a strong relationship between objective and subjective correlations (B=0.71), with overall performance much closer to ideal than if correlations were ignored. Suboptimal evidence weighing reflected subjective misestimates at the encoding level.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 praises the modeling approach: 'the authors show how correlations ought to impact these parameters, and which changes in parameters one would expect to see if participants mis-estimate these correlations or ignore them altogether' and confirms 'they could show that participants in fact performed rational evidence weighting if one assumed that they slightly underestimated the correlation magnitude.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the modelling approach applied to these data showcases an impressively deep understanding of relationships between different parameters of the drift diffusion model.' The editor affirms the model 'will be of use for the study of decision-making.'

results.result: Fit (subjective) correlations were more variable for positive versus negative correlations, possibly reflecting weaker consequences of misestimating positive versus negative correlations on performance.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented as a secondary observation with a speculative interpretation ('possibly reflecting'). No reviewer challenges this claim or its interpretation, and it is consistent with the overall pattern of results that reviewers explicitly support.

results.result: Empirical correlations computed from trial samples were biased toward zero with limited samples, but there was no reliable evidence that participants with shortest RTs had estimates most biased toward zero. Results suggest participants did not compute correlations explicitly on each trial but may have used pattern matching or other heuristics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly identifies this as a weakness: 'While the authors convincingly demonstrate that the observed decision-making behavior seems to stem from a slight underestimation of the correlation magnitudes, their experimental paradigm did not allow them to determine the origin of this bias.' Reviewer 2 similarly notes 'An outstanding question that arises from the current work and remains unanswered here is around the (normative?) origin of the correlation underestimates.' The speculative nature of the heuristics explanation (C57) is acknowledged in the claim itself.

results.result: Participants exhibited learning over the task involving substantial RT decreases with slight accuracy decreases, reflected in higher drift rates and lower decision bounds in the latter half. However, subjective correlation estimates remained stable across task halves, suggesting decisions were based on relatively stable correlation estimates that could be determined and used effectively trial-by-trial.
results.evaluation: These learning effects are presented as secondary analyses supporting the main conclusion about stable correlation sensitivity. No reviewer challenges these findings. The stability of correlation estimates across learning is consistent with the main findings that all reviewers explicitly support.

results.result: The results imply that elapsed time cannot serve as a sole proxy for stimulus strength when observations are correlated. Correlations complicate the relationship between evidence strength and elapsed time, requiring combination with other statistics like correlation. Data are consistent with collapsing bounds for within-correlation adjustments, but collapsing bounds alone could not account for across-correlation behavioral differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly discusses how 'the authors show how correlations ought to impact these parameters' in the DDM framework and confirms the modeling successfully captures behavior. Reviewer 2 praises 'the modelling approach applied to these data showcases an impressively deep understanding of relationships between different parameters of the drift diffusion model.' These mechanistic inferences about collapsing bounds and correlation-dependent adjustments are part of the modeling framework that reviewers explicitly endorse.

results.result: The results contrast with behavioral economics literature showing 'correlation neglect' in high-level decisions. The discrepancy likely results from vast differences in task designs, as decisions based on simple sensory stimuli may rely on different cognitive mechanisms than descriptive scenarios, and direct experience can alleviate correlation neglect.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'As the authors point out in their very well-written paper, appropriate weighting of information gathered in correlated environments has important consequences for real-world decision-making. Yet, while this function has been well studied for 'high-level' (e.g. economic) decisions, how we account for correlations when making simple perceptual decisions on well-controlled behavioural tasks has not been investigated.' This contextualizes and implicitly supports the authors' discussion of differences from economics literature. No reviewer disputes this comparison.

results.result: Prior work on visual cue combination shows some observers assume correlations between within-modality cues, which are thought to be encapsulated in the visual system without conscious access. This suggests the visual system may have specialized mechanisms for computing correlations among visual stimuli that differ from those supporting higher-order cognition.
results.evaluation: This discussion contextualizes the findings within the broader perceptual decision-making literature. Reviewer 2 explicitly praises the work for addressing 'an important and timely question that will be of broad interest to psychologists and neuroscientists' and notes it 'makes strong connections with prior work in different decision-making contexts.' The speculative nature of C85 is acknowledged in the claim itself ('may have'), and no reviewer challenges this contextualization.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on experimental design (C27-C29). Both evaluations find the design theoretically sound and appropriately controlled. OpenEval emphasizes the design controls for confounds; peer review praises how it equalizes evidence across correlations.

Both address trial-by-trial correlation computation (C54, C55, C57). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on statistical evidence, while peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting the paradigm 'did not allow them to determine the origin of this bias' and calling the heuristics explanation speculative.

Perfect agreement on learning effects (C58-C61). Both evaluations support the findings showing dissociation between parameter changes and stable correlation estimates, with no concerns raised about the analyses.

Perfect agreement on comparison to prior literature (C77-C82). Both evaluations support the discussion of differences from economics literature and find the contextualization appropriate, though specific mechanisms remain speculative.
